source: MathlibLemma authors (2026) MathlibLemma: Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics, arXiv 2602.02561
finding: A GPT-5.1 pipeline proposes lemmas from Mathlib seed files, a judge filters them, a formalizer compiles them. The funnel loses a lot at each step.
numbers: Table 1 funnel, 3 domains: proposed 3427/2591/3130 (total 9148); judge-accepted 71.4%/66.6%/63.2% (total 6150); compilable 77.1%/70.6%/61.3% (total 4317); trivial 4.1%/6.6%/10.8%; 4028 non-trivial statements kept. About 44% of proposed lemmas reach the final set.
limits: Generation model is also the judge (GPT-5.1), so the set reflects its taste. One-shot, seed-file local discovery. No downstream-use test.
agent_relevance: Budget for roughly 2 in 5 raw lemma proposals surviving cheap filters. Statement-level filtering before proof attempts saves most compute.

source: MathlibLemma authors (2026) arXiv 2602.02561, judge audit
finding: An LLM judge used as a filter for conjectures is conservative and has poor recall. Many true lemmas are thrown out.
numbers: Audit of 53 judge-rejected candidates: 54% truly false, 46% valid (false negatives).
limits: Small sample (N=53), seed-stratified.
agent_relevance: A cheap LLM plausibility check on a conjecture is a precision tool, not a recall tool. Do not treat its rejection as proof of falsity; use a counterexample search or a prover for that.

source: MathlibLemma authors (2026) arXiv 2602.02561, provability audit and prover results
finding: Most conjectures that provers fail on are still true. Experts proved most of a sample of model-unsolved lemmas. Failures that remain are mostly missing hypotheses.
numbers: Expert open-book audit of 138 model-unsolved lemmas: 107 proved (78%); by domain 79% / 71% / 84%. Of 31 unproven: 25 (81%) missing hypotheses, 5 (16%) false, 1 (3%) formalization gap. Best single model solves about 19%; union of all models 37.39% of 4028. Goedel-Prover-V2-8B Pass@16 only 0.32% (13/4028). Specialized provers do much worse on abstract domains (Kimina 8.24% abstract).
limits: Audit drawn from unsolved residuals, not a random sample. Humans used full Mathlib and AI help.
agent_relevance: Failure to prove a conjecture is weak evidence it is false. The most common defect is a missing side condition, so a refine-the-statement step (add hypothesis) beats discarding.

source: MathlibLemma authors (2026) arXiv 2602.02561, ensemble and downstream limits
finding: Different provers solve different lemmas, so the union nearly doubles coverage. The authors say they did not test whether the new lemmas help later proofs.
numbers: Best single model 19.39% vs union 37.39%. Retrieval-augmented downstream ablation listed as future work. Small subset merged into Mathlib (three examples shown).
limits: Usefulness claimed from expert library-standard judgment, not measured reuse.
agent_relevance: Diverse proposers and provers add coverage. Measure reuse count directly; do not assume that a proven lemma is useful.

source: Alhessi et al. (2025/2026) Lemmanaid: Neuro-Symbolic Lemma Conjecturing, arXiv 2504.04942
finding: Learn lemma templates with a neural net and fill them symbolically. This beats both pure neural generation and the symbolic tool QuickSpec on recovering lemmas that human authors wrote.
numbers: Best backend (DeepSeek-coder-6.7B): 50.2% of gold lemmas on HOL-test, 28.6% AFP-test, 41% AFP-2026. Ensemble with neural baseline 58.6% / 42.7%. Octonions: Lemmanaid 78.9% vs neural 62.3% vs QuickSpec 22.8%; ensemble 84.9%.
limits: Metric is match to human-written gold lemmas, a proxy for usefulness. Gold-match undercounts valid new lemmas.
agent_relevance: Conjecture by analogy to existing lemma shapes (templates) rather than free generation. Reusing a library's own lemma patterns is a strong prior.

source: Alhessi et al. (2025/2026) Lemmanaid, generated conjecture census
finding: Only about 1 in 4 generated conjectures matches a human lemma. Another large share is true but not in the library, and a large share is false or unresolved.
numbers: HOL-test: 7628 conjectures from 4740 gold lemmas. Gold 1721 (22.6%); other true 1356 (17.8%); false 1802 (23.6%); unresolved 2749 (36.0%). Classed with Sledgehammer, Nitpick, Quickcheck.
limits: Unresolved means neither proved nor refuted by the tools, not useless. Best configuration under greedy decoding only.
agent_relevance: Expect about 24% false, 36% unknown. Run a cheap refuter (counterexample) first, then a prover, and keep an explicit unresolved bin.

source: Alhessi et al. (2025/2026) Lemmanaid, commercial LLM comparison and QuickSpec precision
finding: Small fine-tuned models with templates beat frontier commercial LLMs on new, post-cutoff formalizations. QuickSpec floods output with lemmas.
numbers: AFP-2026 (recent, leakage-free): Lemmanaid 6.7B 41.7% vs Neural 6.7B 38.1%; Claude Opus 4.5 19.4% (template) / 34.5% (direct); GPT-5.2 15.8% / 25.2%. Octonions: Opus 47.1%/46.3%, GPT-5.2 50.0%/45.4%. QuickSpec emits several thousand lemmas, precision under 1%.
limits: Commercial models used 5 few-shot examples and about 1700 input tokens. Limited test set (Octonions plus AFP-2026) for cost reasons. Top-5 predictions.
agent_relevance: On unseen material a frontier LLM without library-specific structure is not clearly better. Structure from the library beats raw model size.

source: Xin Huang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: Neural Theorem Proving with Growing Libraries, arXiv 2310.00656
finding: A growing library of verified lemmas, with an evolver that generalizes lemmas, helps a fixed LLM prover. The gain is small and appears late.
numbers: Ablation on miniF2F-valid, 50 attempts per problem: with library 50.4% vs without 47.1% (+3.3 points). Gap near zero early and widens as library grows. Full runs: valid 57.0%, test 50.0% (prior 52.4/45.5). Library reached 22,532 skills.
limits: Ablation done once, only on valid set, 50 attempts, due to cost (about 300 USD per 100-attempt run). Mixed gpt-3.5 versions. No confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Lemma reuse gives a modest, compounding gain. Early library is not worth much, so expect a warm-up cost. Report it with variance.

source: Xin Huang et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover, library composition
finding: Most library entries are generalizations made by an evolver, not lemmas the prover needed. The paper admits some are trivial or already in Isabelle.
numbers: 22,532 skills: 10.8% from prover, 38.2% from evolver request-solver, 51.1% from directional transformation. Skills are deduplicated by embedding distance. Successful proofs use skills either by direct use or by proposing a lemma by imitation (Fig 3b).
quote: some lemmas are trivially true or already exist in Isabelle's theorem library
limits: No count of how many skills were ever retrieved or used. Usefulness shown only by the aggregate ablation and case studies.
agent_relevance: A library can grow 20,000 entries while the used share is unknown. Track use count per lemma and prune; retrieval cost grows with library size.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving, arXiv 2502.00212
finding: Training a conjecturer on conjectures that are barely provable by the current prover gives the prover dense signal. It beats expert iteration at equal sample budget.
numbers: Lean, 48 iterations, 3.6M conjectures, 241M proofs, 51.3B tokens: 28.5% of LeanWorkbook proved vs 13.2% for the prior best expert iteration. miniF2F-test 65.0% (pass@3200), ProofNet-test 23.9%, PutnamBench 8/644. Isabelle run: only 131 of 2.5M proofs for 79K unproved statements were correct, so expert iteration stalls.
limits: Gain measured on the training set LeanWorkbook plus transfer. Some unproved statements are mistranslated, so 100% is not possible. Compute is large.
agent_relevance: Pick conjectures at the edge of current ability (barely provable). Too-hard targets give no signal. This is a selection rule we can copy at inference time.

source: Dong and Ma (2025) STP, transfer ablation
finding: Generated conjectures help outside the set they were made for, but the gain is small.
numbers: Final re-training with the generated conjectures and their proofs gives about 2-3 points higher pass@128 on miniF2F-test and ProofNet-test than re-training on the proved dataset statements alone.
limits: Appendix B.1 only. pass@128, single run reported.
agent_relevance: Transfer of self-generated lemmas is real but small (2-3 points). Do not count on large cross-problem transfer.

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving, arXiv 2507.23726
finding: Lemma-style proving plus a heavy mode that proposes thousands of conjectures, proves them into a lemma pool, ranks and selects hundreds of top lemmas for the main proof. This solved problems the lighter modes could not.
numbers: Heavy setting: 5000 conjectures by default, days of thinking, thousands of lemmas in pool. Past IMO 121/155 (78.1%); by difficulty 47/55 easy, 47/56 medium, 27/44 hard. miniF2F 99.6%; PutnamBench 331/657 vs 86/657 prior best. IMO 2017 P2, 2025 P3 and P4 were proved only under heavy.
quote: empirically, lemmas with low proof rate are often crucial to the final proof
limits: Heavy mode ablation against light is not isolated from model strength. Compute cost very high (days per problem). Lemma score weights not given as numbers.
agent_relevance: The best lemmas are the ones that are hard to prove. Rank by low proof rate, relevance, and length. Easy lemmas are filtered out.

source: Nagashima et al. (2022) Template-Based Conjecturing for Automated Induction in Isabelle/HOL, arXiv 2212.11151
finding: Only 16 fixed, general templates (commutativity, associativity, identity, and the like) create conjectures. Prove them, then use them as auxiliary lemmas. It helps a lot on mid-difficulty induction problems and not on hard ones.
numbers: Largest gain: 40 percentage points on the Prod category. Isaplanner: 60% solved without conjectures, so small gain there. Struggles on TIP15. Proof success reaches 66% after an hour in Prod; about 20% within 5 minutes. Conjecture count does not blow up. Laptop-scale hardware.
limits: Limited to induction in Isabelle, first-order recursive functions. Round count reduced on TIP15 for compute. Baseline is TAP21.
agent_relevance: A small fixed set of generic templates can beat open-ended generation. The gain is concentrated where the lemma is missing but simple.

source: Johansson and Smallbone (2021) Conjectures, Tests and Proofs: An Overview of Theory Exploration (QuickSpec), arXiv 2109.03721
finding: QuickSpec makes equational conjectures by testing terms on random data and keeping only irreducible terms. Output is small and almost never false, but it does not scale.
numbers: Arithmetic example runs in about 5 seconds. Limits: breaks down at libraries of 30+ functions or terms over size about 9. Neural comparison cited: 13-30% of neural-generated statements were both provable and new; the rest were copies, alpha-renamings or false.
quote: It rarely generates any false or duplicate conjectures
limits: Equations only. Needs test generators. Reported by authors of QuickSpec.
agent_relevance: Testing-based filters give high precision. Pair a cheap random-test refuter with every generator; redundancy pruning keeps the set small.

source: Singher and Itzhaky (2020) Theory Exploration Powered By Deductive Synthesis (TheSy), arXiv 2009.04826
finding: Symbolic theory exploration with abstraction finds more lemmas than Hipster and prunes lemmas that are provably redundant. The lemmas speed up inductive proving.
numbers: CVC4 benchmark, 311 problems, 5 min timeout: TheSy exploration plus simple induction proves 187; Z3 75; CVC4 without conjecture generation 70; CVC4 with its own conjecture generation 260. IsaPlanner 85 test cases: TheSy with case split had a better subsumption ratio than Hipster in 65, equal in 6. Time to explore all: TheSy 51.6K s vs Hipster 47.1K s without case split.
limits: CVC4's built-in conjecture generation (260) beat TheSy (187). Larger term depth (k) raises time greatly with few useful lemmas. Case splitting is slow.
agent_relevance: Redundancy by provability (knowledge-subsumption) is a better filter than syntax. Lemma generation has diminishing returns with depth; keep depth bounded.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) Learning-assisted Theorem Proving with Millions of Lemmas, arXiv 1402.3578
finding: Mining millions of intermediate lemmas from HOL Light proofs and adding the best ones helps automated proving only a little in the honest setting.
numbers: Core HOL Light, fully honest evaluation: original success 61.7%, with lemma mining 64.8% (about 5% relative). Best single method Q2 46.2% at 512 premises. Cheating setting (preceding lemma available) 76.5-77.9%. Chained conjecturing of mid-proof lemmas: Q2 from 54.5% (1066) to 61.4% (chain1) and 63.8% (chain2-3), i.e. +12.6% and +17.0% relative. Flyspeck run needed 6 GB memory for about 20 million new intermediate theorems.
limits: The upper bound uses lemmas taken from the proof itself, so it is an oracle. Honest gain depends on how lemmas are scored (PageRank variants, Qi, EQi).
agent_relevance: Lemma quality scores trained on use give a few points. The oracle gap (64.8 vs 77.9) shows that guessing the right mid-proof lemma is the real bottleneck.

source: Kaliszyk and Urban (2014) arXiv 1402.3578, lemma-graph measures
finding: Different usefulness scores pick different lemmas. Size normalization changes the pick strongly.
numbers: First 10,000 lemmas chosen by PageRank PR1 and PR2 overlap 79%. Reverse PageRank PR3 and PR4 overlap only 11%, so PR3 picks bigger lemmas. About 33% of clauses generated from 200,000 core lemmas are subsumed.
limits: HOL Light, ATP-based; not LLM. Usefulness is defined by use in later proofs, not by human judgment.
agent_relevance: Usefulness is a family of measures, not one. Include a size term, or the system picks only huge lemmas.

source: Gauthier and Urban (2025) Learning Conjecturing from Scratch, arXiv 2503.01389
finding: A self-learning loop that conjectures induction predicates, tries them with Z3, and retrains on the ones that worked, starting from zero, solves more than twice as many OEIS problems as strong provers.
numbers: 16,197 OEIS-derived problems. Initial brute force 1000 candidates per problem: 2506 solved. Four runs (260, 60, ... then 99 iterations) reached 5565 total, vs 2265 for CVC5, Vampire or Z3 at 60 s. Table 1, 10 s: Z3 total 4812 with manual induction axioms, CVC5 2702. Loop took 3 months, 2-8 iterations per day.
limits: Predicates trained on own solved problems, so memorization rises as iterations go. Benchmark is narrow (OEIS programs). Heavy compute (4 GPUs, 72 threads).
agent_relevance: Learning from verified successes of one's own conjectures works, with sudden jumps when a useful pattern is found. Rewards: size and speed of the solution.

source: Urban and Jakubuv (2020) First Neural Conjecturing Datasets and Experiments, arXiv 2005.14664
finding: GPT-2 trained on Mizar makes statements that look right but are mostly not useful. Language-model loss does not measure logical usefulness.
numbers: 381,432 predictions, 193,320 unique. 86,899 of the ATP problems were quickly shown countersatisfiable by E. 11,866 proved in 6 s (8105 theorems); 4350 proofs used just the proved theorem itself as a premise.
limits: Early small experiment. Counts the premise-prediction setup, not pure conjecturing. They note their 2016 RNN attempt on Mizar was not convincing.
agent_relevance: Fluent output is not valid output. Always check with a prover or refuter; leakage (restating the goal) must be detected.

source: Gamboa, Manolios, Smith, Thompson (2023) Using Counterexample Generation and Theory Exploration to Suggest Missing Hypotheses (DrLA), arXiv 2311.08857
finding: When a conjectured theorem is false, theory exploration restricted to non-redundant terms can suggest the missing hypothesis. It works on type-like hypotheses and fails when the needed predicate is not in the vocabulary.
numbers: Tested by removing hypotheses from Community Books theorems. Case: suggests (consp x) for (< 0 (len x)); suggests (atom x) for a conclusion-only query. Failure: subsumption heuristic picked hypotheses too weak for a real-number case (x = 1/2 counterexample).
limits: ACL2 only. Case-study evidence, not a rate over a corpus.
agent_relevance: Pairs with MathlibLemma (81% of failures were missing hypotheses): refine a false conjecture by searching hypotheses that exclude the counterexamples.

source: Ritchie and Hanna (1984) AM: a case study in AI methodology, Artificial Intelligence 23(3), via search and Wikipedia summary
finding: The critics found AM's published account hid much of the discovery work. Heuristics were mixed into control code, rules were vague, and user hints steered it. A reader could not rebuild it from the paper.
numbers: No counts in the source beyond Lenat's claim of hundreds of concepts and hundreds of heuristic rules. Cited rules: Rule 2 (boost topics user mentioned), Rule 218 (vague 'structurally similar').
limits: Read through Wikipedia summary and a search result, not the 1984 paper itself. Lenat's rebuttal classes the difficulties as omitted heuristics and miscommunication.
agent_relevance: Claims of discovery from a conjecturing system need reconstruction tests. Log which prompt hints pushed the agent toward a result.

source: Lenat and Brown (1984) Why AM and EURISKO appear to work, Artificial Intelligence 23(3)
finding: Lenat and Brown say AM's power came from heuristics, and that it stalled because it could not discover new heuristics for the new fields it opened. They concede that random short Lisp programs can be read as sophisticated concepts.
numbers: Not given in the source seen (abstract and search snippets).
limits: Only a search snippet and the Wikipedia summary were seen. Not a full read.
agent_relevance: Rival explanation for AM: interestingness came from the representation (short programs are often meaningful) and the observer. Test the agent's conjecture quality against random baselines.

source: Ritchie (1991) Learning from AM, Edinburgh DAI report rp522
finding: Seven years on, almost no work had built on AM, and there were no reported replications. The paper asks why AM looked so impressive and was hard to extend.
numbers: None. Only the abstract is online ('NO ONLINE COPY').
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Failure to replicate is itself evidence. A scaffold should ship with its full spec and logs so others can rerun it.

source: Davila (2024) The Optimist: Towards Fully Automated Graph Theory Research, arXiv 2411.09158 (Graffiti background)
finding: Graffiti's Dalmatian heuristic keeps a conjecture only if it holds on all stored examples and gives a sharper bound than earlier ones on at least one. This keeps counts low, and limits come from the example set.
numbers: Graffiti used a few hundred graphs; Graffiti.pc used up to millions, but a bigger set did not always give better conjectures because small special counterexample graphs were missing. Optimist with a tiny knowledge base produced nearly 60 broad conjectures. Many Graffiti conjectures led to published papers (cited refs 6-31, chemistry 32-39).
quote: increasing the dataset size did not always yield higher quality conjectures
limits: Survey inside a systems paper. No proved or refuted tally.
agent_relevance: Conjecture quality depends on the example set. Keep a small zoo of special cases and edge cases as counterexample probes.

source: Davila (2026) Automated Conjecturing with TxGraffiti, arXiv 2409.19379
finding: Conjectures here are table-true inequalities fitted by small linear programs, then ranked by touch and sharpness and pruned for redundancy. They are true only on the table, so they need proof.
numbers: No proof-rate figure in the abstract; the system outputs a compact ranked set per target invariant.
limits: Only the abstract and header were read for this item. Table-true is not truth.
agent_relevance: Rank by informativeness (sharp on some case) and remove implied ones before spending proof effort.

source: Colton (2001/2002) Automated Theory Formation in Pure Mathematics (HR), publisher and thesis summaries
finding: HR forms concepts, conjectures them from examples, tries to prove with Otter and disprove with Mace. The publisher says 20 new number types it invented were accepted into the Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences.
numbers: 20 sequences accepted (promotional blurb only, unverified). Later HR work: dozens of example algebras, hundreds of concepts, thousands of conjectures.
limits: Only search snippets seen; claim comes from the publisher, not the OEIS.
agent_relevance: Prover plus model-finder as a pair (prove or refute) is the standard filter we should copy.

source: Graffiti history (DeLaVina) and secondary blog via search
finding: Graffiti conjectures inspired about eighty papers. A blog says at least 60 were proved by mathematicians. Neither figure was checked.
numbers: About 80 papers; at least 60 proved (secondary, unverified).
limits: Search snippet only. Papers inspired is not the same as conjectures proved. No refutation tally found.
agent_relevance: Even the most cited conjecturer has no clean precision figure. Do not expect a published usefulness rate for classic systems.
